summary: Proposes TFRC-SP, a variant of TCP Friendly Rate Control for applications that send small packets, such as voice. It is for further experimentation only, not widespread deployment. This RFC is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Some apps send many tiny packets. This proposes a rule for how fast they can send while still sharing fairly with TCP. It is only a test idea for now.

questions: tcp friendly rate control for small packets
subtitle: A tweak to TCP-friendly rate control so voice-style traffic with small packets is not slowed unfairly.

tldr.problem: TFRC counts its rate in packets per round-trip time, so a low-bandwidth flow with small packets can be forced to slow down next to large-packet TCP flows, even when its bytes per second are lower.
tldr.mechanism: TFRC-SP assumes a nominal segment size of 1460 bytes, reduces the allowed rate to account for 40 bytes of headers, counts every lost packet in short loss intervals, and enforces a minimum interval of 10 ms between packets.
tldr.outcome: Small-packet flows get about the same bytes per second as a 1460-byte TCP flow at the same drop rate. Where small packets are dropped less often than large ones, TFRC-SP can take considerably more than its share, so it is for experimentation only.

today: RFC 4828 is an Experimental RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text says it is for further experimentation and not for widespread deployment in the global Internet, and that a DCCP congestion control ID based on TFRC-SP would be specified in a separate document.

sections.title: Why a Small-Packet Variant
sections.content:
TFRC-SP is an experimental small-packet variant of TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC, RFC 3448). TFRC aims at fairness with TCP while avoiding abrupt rate changes, which suits streaming media. But it uses a rate in packets per round-trip time, so a low-bandwidth flow of small packets sharing a bottleneck with large-packet TCP flows may be forced to slow down even though its bytes per second are below TCP's.

That would be fair only if the network limit were in packets per second rather than bytes per second. The RFC follows RFC 3714, which argues it is acceptable for VoIP flows to assume the limit is in bytes per second and to match the rate of a TCP flow with 1500-byte packets at the same packet drop rate.

TFRC-SP is meant for flows sending packets of less than 1500 bytes with at least 10 ms between packets. The RFC warns about encouraging a large deployment of best-effort traffic consisting entirely of small packets, and so keeps incentives for larger packets. RFC 3448 had promised a later variant called TFRC-PS for applications that vary packet size; this document specifies TFRC-SP instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal rules punish apps that send many tiny messages. This version judges them by how much they send in total, not by how many messages.

sections.title: What TFRC-SP Changes
sections.content:
TFRC-SP changes four things relative to TFRC.

  • Nominal segment size. The segment size s in the throughput equation defaults to 1460 bytes. If the endpoint knows the path MTU and the derived MSS is below 1460 bytes, it SHOULD use the MSS; if the MSS is below 536 bytes, it MUST. Knowing the path MTU is not required.
  • Header accounting. The allowed rate is reduced by X := X * s_true / (s_true + H), with H set to the constant 40 bytes. With 40-byte data segments the rate would be halved. A connection MAY use a more precise H, such as 32 bytes for DCCP over IPv4 without options.
  • Loss counting in high loss. In short loss intervals, those of at most two round-trip times, every lost or marked packet counts, not just one loss event.
  • Minimum interval. TFRC-SP enforces a Min Interval of 10 ms between packets. A flow that wants to exceed this limit MUST use the conventional TFRC equations.

The effect is that, apart from the cap of 100 packets per second, a TFRC-SP flow gets the same bytes per second as a TCP flow with 1460-byte segments at the same drop rate.
sections.plainLanguage: The app pretends its messages are big ones for fairness, pays a small fee for the envelopes, and cannot send faster than 100 messages a second.

sections.title: Counting Loss in Short Loss Intervals
sections.content:
Standard TFRC and TCP respond to at most one loss event per round-trip time, which works because they cannot keep sending many packets per RTT under heavy loss. A TFRC-SP flow could be sending many small packets where TCP would send one large packet, so counting only loss events would let it ignore heavy congestion.

For a short loss interval with N packets including K lost or marked packets, TFRC-SP sets the interval length to N/K instead of N. The loss event rate then becomes K/N instead of 1/N. The average is still taken over the eight most recent intervals.

Because the length of a short interval can change as more losses are detected, TFRC-SP also adds a rule: the current loss interval may be included in the average only if more than two round-trip times have passed since it began. This is meant to prevent needless oscillations. After the first loss event, TFRC-SP also uses 1460 bytes, not the real segment size, when it seeds the loss history.
sections.plainLanguage: When lots of tiny messages are lost in a short time, the app counts every lost one, so it notices real trouble and slows down.

sections.title: Design Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The header factor gives applications a reason to use fewer, larger packets. For example, a sender using 120-byte packets needs a TCP-friendly rate of 128 Kbps to send 96 Kbps of application data. The Min Interval adds another guard, because small packets also load routers that are limited in packets per second. The RFC says VoIP applications that send at most one packet every 10 ms are not affected. It admits nothing stops a flow from opening multiple connections, just as nothing stops it from using UDP or parallel TCP connections.

The nominal size of 1460 bytes can mismatch the path. On a path with an MSS of only 536 bytes, a TFRC-SP flow could receive almost three times the bandwidth of a TCP flow, and with an MSS near 4000 bytes a TCP flow could get almost three times as much. The RFC accepts factors of two or three. TFRC-SP is not recommended for transport protocols that keep no knowledge of the path MTU.

TFRC-SP can also be used by applications that keep a fixed packet rate and shrink packet size under congestion. Since the allowed rate is in bytes per second, there is little room to game it by changing packet size. Details of adaptive use are left to application-specific documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are a bit rough on purpose. Being off by two or three times is fine, as long as nobody grabs the whole road.

sections.title: Where It Works and Where It Overreaches
sections.content:
The RFC reports simulations. When large and small packets see similar packet drop rates, TFRC-SP gives roughly the desired rate. When every byte is equally likely to be dropped, standard TFRC already gives reasonable fairness between small-packet and large-packet flows.

When small packets are less likely to be dropped than large ones, TFRC-SP is not fair: small-packet flows can receive considerably more bandwidth, and in some cases large-packet TCP flows can be essentially starved. The RFC names Drop-Tail queues measured in bytes and active queue management in byte mode as such settings, and says it has been reported that wireless links sometimes pass small packets that larger ones cannot. For this reason the RFC says TFRC-SP is not intended for widespread deployment in the global Internet at this time.

Compared with RFC 3714, which only tells a fixed-rate telephony flow to stop when drop rates exceed a threshold, TFRC-SP lets a small-packet flow cut its rate moderately as drops rise.
sections.plainLanguage: It works well when big and small letters get lost equally often. If small letters rarely get lost, the small sender gets more than its fair share.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no new security considerations. TFRC-SP is not a transport protocol itself but a congestion control mechanism used with one, so security mostly depends on that transport protocol. As for TFRC in RFC 3448, a transport using TFRC-SP needs to protect against spoofed feedback and against incorrect information from the receiver, and protocols using ECN will want the ECN nonce.
sections.plainLanguage: It adds no new security problems, but the app using it still has to stop fake messages from fooling the sender.
